course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Consequences of Industrialization
unit.description: Study why industrial states built empires, how colonized peoples resisted, how economies were reshaped, and why millions of people migrated.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.3 key concept: resistance to imperial rule included rebellions, such as the 1857 rebellion in India
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Indian Rebellion of 1857
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1857, sepoys in the East India Company's army mutinied after rumors spread that new rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat, which offended both Hindu and Muslim soldiers. The revolt drew on deeper grievances: lands taken by the company, heavy taxes, and fears that British rule threatened Indian religions and customs.

Rebels restored the aging Mughal emperor in Delhi as a symbol of resistance. British forces crushed the rebellion by 1858 with great brutality. The British government then ended company rule, exiled the last Mughal emperor, and governed India directly.

questions.prompt: Rebels' restoration of the Mughal emperor most likely served to
choices: invite British forces to negotiate
show loyalty to the East India Company
give the revolt a symbol of British royal authority in India
give the revolt a symbol of legitimate Indian authority
questions.explanation: The Mughal emperor represented older Indian sovereignty.
choiceExplanations: The Mughal emperor represented older Indian sovereignty.
questions.distinguisher: The emperor symbolized Indian, not British, authority.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.3 key concept: resistance to imperialism, including Ethiopia's successful defense of its independence
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing Ethiopia's victory at Adwa in 1896
stimulusBlocks.text:
Emperor Menelik II of Ethiopia bought modern rifles and artillery from European suppliers in the 1880s and 1890s and built a large, well-armed army. When Italy invaded, Ethiopian forces defeated the Italian army at the Battle of Adwa in 1896.

The victory forced Italy to recognize Ethiopia's independence. Ethiopia became a symbol of African resistance, and it was one of only two African states that remained independent during the partition of the continent.

questions.distinguisher: The Indian Rebellion was crushed; Ethiopia succeeded.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.3 key concept: religious movements, such as the Ghost Dance and the Xhosa cattle-killing movement, were among responses to imperial expansion
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, comparing two religious responses to colonial expansion, 1856–1890
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1856, a young Xhosa woman named Nongqawuse in southern Africa reported a prophecy: if the Xhosa killed their cattle and destroyed their crops, their ancestors would return and drive the British into the sea. Many followed the prophecy. The result was a famine in which tens of thousands died, and the British took more Xhosa land.

In the 1880s, the Ghost Dance spread among Native American peoples of the western United States. Followers believed the dance would restore the buffalo and the old way of life. In 1890, US troops killed more than 250 Lakota people at Wounded Knee.

choices: That joining a Christian mission would protect their villages

That water blessed by a spirit would turn German bullets to water

choiceExplanations: The passage names a spirit medium's blessed water, not Christian missions, as the uniting belief.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.3 key concept: indigenous peoples resisted imperial expansion through armed and religious movements
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Maji Maji Rebellion, 1905–1907
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1905 people in German East Africa, in what is now Tanzania, rose against colonial rule. German officials had imposed taxes payable in cash and forced villagers to grow cotton for export on communal plots, work that took time from food crops. A spirit medium named Kinjikitile Ngwale taught that water blessed by a spirit, maji in Swahili, would turn German bullets to water.

People from many different ethnic groups joined the rebellion, which spread across a large region. German forces used machine guns and then destroyed crops and villages to starve the rebels, and historians estimate that between 100,000 and 300,000 Africans died, most from famine. After the rebellion, German officials reduced the worst abuses of forced labor.

questions.prompt: Which German colonial policy most directly helped trigger the rebellion?
choices: A ban on missionary schools in the colony
A requirement that villagers move into German-built towns
The seizure of all firearms owned by villagers
Forced growing of cotton for export along with cash taxes
questions.explanation: The passage says officials imposed cash taxes and forced villagers to grow cotton on communal plots.
choiceExplanations: The passage does not mention missionary schools.
The passage blames forced cotton growing and cash taxes, not resettlement.
The passage does not mention disarmament.
The passage says officials imposed cash taxes and forced villagers to grow cotton on communal plots.
questions.distinguisher: Colonial governments often disarmed local populations, but the cause named here was forced labor.
